Their affair ends abruptly when she mysteriously disappears. Eight years later, Michael is a law student. One day, while observing Nazi war criminals on trial, he's shocked to find Hanna as a defendant in the courtroom. The court finds her guilty of killing 300 Jewish women during the war and sentences her to life in prison. While behind bars, Michael sends her books on tape, which, over time, help Hanna finally learn to read. Therein lies the problem for Rosenbaum. "What essentially it did," said Rosenbaum, "was celebrate the enrichment of a life of a mass murderer when she learned how to read. ... Imagine if there were a film about Charles Manson learning how to play chess and what a better guy it made him." However, others in the Jewish community are applauding the film, including Ken Jacobson, deputy national director of the Anti-Defamation League. Jacobson says "The Reader" opens itself up to criticism, but is worthy of an Oscar at the same time. "I think it conveys a series of messages that actually are very powerful about the Holocaust, and it's not in the usual way," Jacobson told CNN. "As time goes on, as we have Holocaust deniers emerging more and more, we need people to be able to relate personally to what happened," said Jacobson. "I think this film does this in a very powerful way." The Weinstein Company, the studio behind "The Reader," says it is proud of the film. "It is sad that some people misinterpreted the film's message," the company said in a statement. "It is not about the Holocaust," the company added, "it is about what Germany did to itself and its future generations." Will Rosenbaum's piece, and the backlash he touched off, affect "The Reader's" Oscar chances Sunday? Entertainment reporter Tom O'Neil, who follows awards shows for the Los Angeles Times' TheEnvelope.com, doesn't think so. Given "The Reader's" five nominations, he believes Hollywood has already embraced the film. "Oscar has taken special notice of 'The Reader' because it's not just your average Holocaust movie," said O'Neil. "It doesn't beg for forgiveness when dealing with Nazis. It makes you think." Still, Rosenbaum says any further accolades for the drama would be unfortunate. "I would be very disappointed in the intelligence level of Hollywood if it gave the best picture award to 'The Reader,' " he said.

**LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) —** One major contender’s chances of winning Oscar gold may be harmed by its sensitive subject matter.

*The Reader*, nominated for five Oscars—including Best Actress for star Kate Winslet and Best Picture—is being condemned by *Explaining Hitler* author Ron Rosenbaum. He has urged Academy members to shun the post-World War II drama because, he says, the film “asks us to empathize with an unrepentant mass murderer.”

Rosenbaum, who wrote his commentary for Slate.com, said that is not his only objection.

“It gives the impression that ordinary German people only learned the terrible things that happened in the death camps in the East after the war,” he said in an interview with CNN. “In fact, ordinary German people participated in Hitler’s final solution, the extermination of the Jews—it was no secret.”

Read Rosenbaum’s essay.

Based on the German book of the same title, *The Reader* stars Winslet as Hanna Schmitz, a former Nazi prison guard living in postwar Germany. She meets teenager Michael Berg (David Cross), and the two begin a secret affair. At Hanna’s request, Michael often reads aloud to her. Unbeknownst to him, Hanna is illiterate.

Their affair ends abruptly when she mysteriously disappears.

Eight years later, Michael is a law student. One day, while observing the trial of Nazi war criminals, he is shocked to discover Hanna among the defendants. The court finds her guilty of killing 300 Jewish women during the war and sentences her to life in prison.

While Hanna is behind bars, Michael sends her books on tape, which eventually help her learn to read.

Therein lies the problem for Rosenbaum.

“What essentially it did,” Rosenbaum said, “was celebrate the enrichment of a life of a mass murderer when she learned how to read. ... Imagine if there were a film about Charles Manson learning how to play chess and what a better guy it made him.”

Others in the Jewish community, however, have applauded the film, including Ken Jacobson, deputy national director of the Anti-Defamation League. Jacobson says *The Reader* leaves itself open to criticism but is, at the same time, worthy of an Oscar.

“I think it conveys a series of messages that actually are very powerful about the Holocaust, and it’s not in the usual way,” Jacobson told CNN.

“As time goes on, as we have Holocaust deniers emerging more and more, we need people to be able to relate personally to what happened,” he said. “I think this film does this in a very powerful way.”

The Weinstein Company, the studio behind *The Reader*, says it is proud of the film.

“It is sad that some people misinterpreted the film’s message,” the company said in a statement. “It is not about the Holocaust,” the statement added. “It is about what Germany did to itself and its future generations.”

Will Rosenbaum’s commentary—and the backlash it ignited—affect *The Reader*’s Oscar prospects on Sunday?

Entertainment reporter Tom O’Neil, who covers awards shows for the Los Angeles Times’ TheEnvelope.com, does not think so. Given *The Reader*’s five nominations, he believes Hollywood has already embraced the film.

“Oscar has taken special notice of *The Reader* because it’s not just your average Holocaust movie,” O’Neil said. “It doesn’t beg for forgiveness when dealing with Nazis. It makes you think.”

Still, Rosenbaum says any further accolades for the drama would be unfortunate.

“I would be very disappointed in the intelligence level of Hollywood if it gave the Best Picture award to *The Reader*,” he said.

The post-World War II drama has earned five Oscar nominations, among them best picture and best actress for Winslet. However, Ron Rosenbaum, author of *Explaining Hitler*, has urged Academy voters not to support it. In a commentary published on Slate.com, Rosenbaum argued that the movie encourages audiences to feel sympathy for a mass killer who never expressed remorse.

That is not Rosenbaum’s only objection. Speaking with CNN, he said the film wrongly suggests that average Germans did not discover the horrors committed in the eastern death camps until the war had ended. In reality, he maintained, ordinary Germans took part in Hitler’s “final solution”—the murder of Europe’s Jews—and the extermination campaign was not hidden from the public.

Adapted from the German novel of the same name, *The Reader* features Winslet as Hanna Schmitz, a onetime Nazi prison guard living in Germany after the war. She begins a clandestine relationship with a teenager, Michael Berg, played by David Cross. At Hanna’s request, Michael frequently reads books aloud to her, unaware that she cannot read.

Their relationship suddenly ends when Hanna disappears without explanation. Eight years afterward, Michael—now studying law—attends the trial of accused Nazi war criminals and is stunned to see Hanna among the defendants. She is convicted of causing the deaths of 300 Jewish women during the war and receives a life sentence.

While Hanna is imprisoned, Michael sends her recordings of books. By listening to the tapes, she gradually teaches herself to read.

For Rosenbaum, that part of the story is precisely the issue. He said the movie effectively celebrates the way literacy improves the life of a mass murderer. He compared the idea to making a film in which Charles Manson learns chess and supposedly becomes a better person because of it.

Not everyone in the Jewish community shares Rosenbaum’s view. Ken Jacobson, deputy national director of the Anti-Defamation League, has praised the movie. Although he acknowledged that *The Reader* leaves itself vulnerable to criticism, he also said it deserves consideration for an Oscar.

According to Jacobson, the film communicates several unusually powerful ideas about the Holocaust. As Holocaust denial becomes increasingly common over time, he said, people need ways to connect personally with what occurred. In his opinion, *The Reader* accomplishes that with considerable force.

The Weinstein Company, which released the movie, also defended it and said it was proud of the production. In a statement, the studio expressed regret that some viewers had misunderstood the film’s meaning. The company said the story is not specifically about the Holocaust; rather, it examines the damage Germany inflicted on itself and on generations that followed.

Whether Rosenbaum’s article and the controversy it generated will influence the movie’s Oscar performance on Sunday remains uncertain. Tom O’Neil, an entertainment journalist who covers awards for the Los Angeles Times website TheEnvelope.com, does not expect the backlash to make a difference.

Because *The Reader* received five nominations, O’Neil believes the film industry has already accepted it. He said the Academy singled it out because it is not a conventional Holocaust drama: instead of asking viewers to forgive Nazis, it challenges them to think.

Rosenbaum nevertheless said he would consider any additional honors for the film regrettable. If *The Reader* were named best picture, he said, he would be deeply disappointed by what that decision suggested about Hollywood’s judgment.

The Editor works quietly between the writer and the Reader. One shapes raw thoughts into clear sentences; the other gives those sentences meaning.

An Editor searches for what is hidden beneath awkward phrases, unnecessary words, and uncertain ideas. The goal is not to replace the writer’s voice, but to help it travel farther. Every correction is a small act of attention: a question about rhythm, clarity, purpose, or truth.

The Reader sees none of this invisible work. They simply open the page and enter. If the Editor has succeeded, the path feels natural. The Reader moves from sentence to sentence without noticing the bridges that were repaired or the obstacles that were removed.

Yet the Reader is never passive. Each person brings memories, expectations, and emotions to a text. In this way, writing is completed twice: first by the Editor, who prepares it, and then by the Reader, who brings it to life.

# Oscar nominee ‘The Reader’ sparks debate over its portrayal of a Nazi guard

**By CNN Entertainment**

The Oscar-nominated drama “The Reader” has drawn acclaim for Kate Winslet’s performance, but it is also facing sharp criticism over its depiction of a former Nazi concentration-camp guard.

The film, adapted from Bernhard Schlink’s novel, follows a postwar German teenager who has an affair with an older woman, Hanna Schmitz, played by Winslet. Years later, he discovers that Hanna served as a guard at a concentration camp and is on trial for her role in the deaths of Jewish prisoners.

“The Reader” received five Academy Award nominations, including best picture, best director and best actress. Yet its awards-season success has intensified a dispute over whether the story humanizes a perpetrator at the expense of her victims.

Writer and critic Ron Rosenbaum delivered one of the strongest attacks, arguing in Slate that the movie shifts attention away from Holocaust victims and toward the emotional burdens of Germans. He said Hanna’s illiteracy is used as a device that risks softening the audience’s judgment of her crimes and described the film as morally confused.

Rosenbaum also criticized the movie for turning the Holocaust into a backdrop for a story about guilt, shame and sexual obsession. In his view, the film invites viewers to pity Hanna without adequately confronting the choices she made as a camp guard.

The Anti-Defamation League rejected the suggestion that “The Reader” excuses Nazi crimes. Abraham H. Foxman, then the organization’s national director and a Holocaust survivor, said the film does not absolve Hanna of responsibility. The ADL argued that the story examines the struggle of postwar Germans to understand the actions of the previous generation while still presenting Hanna as accountable for her conduct.

The Weinstein Company, which distributed the film in the United States, also defended the picture. The company said the movie neither minimizes the Holocaust nor asks audiences to forgive Hanna. Instead, it characterized the film as an exploration of individual responsibility, secrecy and the legacy of Nazi-era crimes.

Supporters have made a similar distinction, noting that Hanna’s illiteracy explains some of her behavior but does not excuse her decision to participate in persecution or her failure to prevent prisoners from dying. They say the discomfort created by the character is central to the film’s moral questions.

The controversy reflects a broader argument that has long surrounded movies about the Holocaust: whether depicting perpetrators as complex human beings deepens historical understanding or risks generating sympathy that obscures their victims.

For “The Reader,” the debate has become part of its Oscar narrative. Even as Winslet’s performance and the film’s craftsmanship have been praised, critics and advocates continue to disagree over whether its central perspective illuminates Germany’s reckoning with the Holocaust—or places the emotional focus in the wrong place.

## *The Reader* Continues to Stir Debate Over Holocaust Guilt and Postwar Germany

**SPOILER WARNING: This report reveals major plot developments and the ending of *The Reader*.**

Bernhard Schlink’s novel *The Reader*, later adapted into an Oscar-winning film, follows Michael Berg, a German teenager who begins an affair in the 1950s with Hanna Schmitz, a much older tram conductor. During their secret meetings, Hanna asks Michael to read literature aloud to her. She eventually disappears without explanation.

Years later, while studying law, Michael encounters Hanna again when he attends the trial of former Nazi concentration-camp guards. Hanna is accused of helping select prisoners for death and of allowing women to burn inside a locked church during a forced evacuation. Although several defendants share responsibility, Hanna accepts blame for writing a damaging report rather than reveal that she is illiterate.

She receives a life sentence. Michael, realizing her secret, does not intervene. Decades later, he sends her recordings of himself reading books, enabling her to teach herself to read and write. Hanna is eventually granted parole, but she kills herself shortly before her release. She leaves money for a Jewish survivor of the camp, who refuses to treat it as absolution and asks that it be donated to a literacy organization.

Supporters of the work say it offers a powerful portrait of postwar Germany’s moral inheritance. Michael’s mixture of shame, love, judgment and emotional paralysis is often read as representing a younger generation struggling with crimes committed by parents and authority figures. From this perspective, Hanna’s illiteracy does not excuse her actions; instead, it shows how personal weakness, secrecy and obedience can coexist with—and help enable—atrocity.

Critics argue that the story risks shifting sympathy toward a perpetrator while giving comparatively little attention to victims. They contend that Hanna’s illiteracy can function as a mitigating device, inviting audiences to see her as ashamed, vulnerable or trapped rather than fully responsible for her choices. Some also object to framing Holocaust guilt through Michael’s romantic and psychological suffering, saying it can make German discomfort more central than Jewish experience.

The opposing view is that this discomfort is precisely the point: Michael cannot reconcile private intimacy with historical judgment, and Hanna’s limitations never erase her participation in mass murder. The survivor’s refusal to validate Hanna’s attempted restitution reinforces the idea that remorse cannot undo the crime.

The debate has helped make *The Reader* both influential and contentious: a work praised for confronting inherited guilt, yet criticized for the emotional and narrative space it grants a former Nazi guard.

## Rosenbaum Urges Oscar Voters to Reject *The Reader* as Supporters Defend Its Unconventional Holocaust Story

As Academy members prepared to cast their ballots, critic and author Ron Rosenbaum launched an impassioned campaign against *The Reader*, arguing that the Oscar-nominated drama turns a Holocaust perpetrator into an object of misplaced sympathy.

The film, directed by Stephen Daldry and adapted by David Hare from Bernhard Schlink’s novel, follows Michael Berg, a German teenager who has an affair with an older woman, Hanna Schmitz. Years later, Michael discovers that Hanna—played by Kate Winslet—served as a guard at a Nazi concentration camp and took part in the deaths of Jewish prisoners.

Writing in *Slate*, Rosenbaum urged Oscar voters not to honor the film, particularly in the best-picture category. His central objection was that *The Reader* uses Hanna’s illiteracy to soften the audience’s judgment of her crimes. By presenting her as ashamed, emotionally damaged and vulnerable, he argued, the film risks shifting attention away from the victims and toward the suffering of a perpetrator.

For Rosenbaum, that is not simply a dramatic miscalculation. It is a moral distortion. He contended that the film encourages viewers to treat Hanna’s inability to read as a hidden tragedy that rivals—or even helps explain—her participation in mass murder. The result, in his view, is a form of sentimentality that confuses personal weakness with diminished responsibility.

Supporters of *The Reader*, however, say that discomfort is precisely the point. Schlink has described the story’s central question as: “How can you love someone who has done something terribly wrong?” Admirers argue that the film does not absolve Hanna but instead examines how intimacy, guilt and historical knowledge collide.

Roger Ebert framed the film’s challenge in similarly direct terms, asking “how much sympathy” an audience can feel for someone guilty of a horrific crime. For defenders, the willingness to pose that question distinguishes *The Reader* from more conventional Holocaust dramas. The film does not offer Hanna’s illiteracy as an acquittal, they say, but as one element in a portrait of a morally compromised person.

Others have emphasized the story’s focus on postwar Germany. Michael’s shock and shame reflect the experience of a younger generation forced to confront the crimes of parents, teachers and lovers. From that perspective, *The Reader* is less about redeeming a former guard than about the corrosive legacy of concealed guilt. As Hare has explained in discussing the adaptation, the story concerns “a generation coming to terms with what the previous generation did.”

Winslet’s supporters also point to the severity of her performance. Hanna is not portrayed as secretly heroic or falsely accused. She admits serving as a guard, displays a chilling obedience to authority and fails to express remorse in ways audiences may expect. Her illiteracy makes her more psychologically legible, defenders argue, but not innocent.

The dispute ultimately turns on what it means to humanize a perpetrator. Rosenbaum sees the film’s focus on Hanna’s vulnerability as an invitation to moral equivalence and emotional exoneration. Supporters answer that recognizing a criminal’s humanity is not the same as forgiving her—and that portraying Nazi perpetrators only as incomprehensible monsters can obscure the ordinary choices and social structures that made their crimes possible.

That tension has made *The Reader* one of the awards season’s most contentious films. Its admirers call it “powerful” because it refuses a reassuring division between monsters and victims, and “unconventional” because it examines the Holocaust through memory, sexuality and generational shame. Rosenbaum believes those same choices dangerously displace the people who suffered most.

His appeal to Oscar voters therefore goes beyond questions of cinematic quality. It asks whether honoring *The Reader* would reward moral complexity or confer prestige on a story that, in his judgment, extends compassion in the wrong direction.

# ‘The Reader’ and the Oscars: When Empathy for a Nazi Character Becomes an Ethical Flashpoint

When *The Reader* arrived in theaters in late 2008, it came packaged as the kind of prestige drama Hollywood often embraces: a best-selling novel, an acclaimed director, an awards-season release and a formidable performance by Kate Winslet. But its ascent to five Academy Award nominations—including best picture—turned the film into something larger and more contentious: a debate over whether humanizing a former Nazi concentration-camp guard deepens historical understanding or dangerously redirects sympathy away from her victims.

Directed by Stephen Daldry and adapted by David Hare from Bernhard Schlink’s 1995 novel, *The Reader* follows Michael Berg, a German teenager who begins an affair with Hanna Schmitz, an older woman played by Winslet. Years later, while studying law, Michael discovers that Hanna is on trial with other former guards for crimes committed during the Holocaust. Among the allegations is that the women allowed Jewish prisoners to die in a burning church rather than unlock the doors.

Michael also realizes that Hanna is illiterate—a secret she protects so fiercely that she accepts disproportionate responsibility for a written report rather than admit she could not have authored it.

That revelation is the source of the film’s dramatic power and its ethical peril.

## Five Oscar nominations—and a larger argument

At the 81st Academy Awards, *The Reader* received nominations for:

- Best Picture  
- Best Director for Stephen Daldry  
- Best Actress for Kate Winslet  
- Best Adapted Screenplay for David Hare  
- Best Cinematography for Roger Deakins and Chris Menges  

Winslet won best actress, securing her first Oscar after five previous nominations. Her victory capped a season in which she was also widely praised for *Revolutionary Road*, but it was *The Reader* that ultimately became her Academy Award vehicle.

The nominations, particularly the best-picture recognition, amplified an already fierce critical dispute. Some viewers saw a morally serious film about postwar Germany, generational guilt and the difficulty of understanding a person without absolving her. Others argued that its narrative structure asked audiences to regard Hanna’s illiteracy as a hidden wound—and, by extension, as an explanation that competes with the enormity of her crimes.

The central objection was not simply that Hanna is portrayed as human. Serious art has long examined perpetrators as human beings rather than as abstractions. The concern was where the film places its emotional weight.

Hanna’s shame, loneliness and vulnerability receive intimate attention. The Jewish women who died under her watch remain largely outside the frame, while Michael’s emotional devastation becomes the story’s principal moral lens. For critics, that imbalance risks transforming a Holocaust narrative into a tragedy about a perpetrator’s secret and the burden it places on a German man who loved her.

## Illiteracy as context—or narrative exoneration?

The film never declares Hanna innocent. She admits that she was a guard, acknowledges selecting prisoners and responds to questions about the church fire with chilling practical logic: the guards could not release the prisoners because they might escape.

Yet *The Reader* surrounds those admissions with a revelation designed to alter the audience’s understanding of her. Her illiteracy explains why she asks Michael to read aloud, why she leaves jobs when promotion threatens to expose her and why she refuses to defend herself effectively at trial.

Defenders of the film argue that explanation is not exoneration. Hanna’s inability to read does not force her to join the SS, select prisoners for death or leave people locked inside a burning building. If anything, the film’s contrast between social vulnerability and moral responsibility makes her more disturbing: a person can be disadvantaged, ashamed and emotionally damaged while still being responsible for monstrous acts.

On that reading, *The Reader* resists the comforting idea that perpetrators must be inhuman. Hanna is capable of tenderness, desire and embarrassment, but none of those qualities cancels what she did. Empathy becomes a method of scrutiny, not a pardon.

Critics counter that movies do not communicate only through explicit judgments. They also guide viewers through screen time, music, close-ups, romantic imagery and narrative revelation. Hanna’s illiteracy is staged as the story’s great secret, and Michael treats exposing it as a betrayal. That structure can make the audience feel that her deepest humiliation is not participation in mass murder but being unable to read.

The moral hierarchy is therefore unstable. The film may insist that Hanna remains guilty, but its emotional machinery can suggest that she is also a victim—of poverty, shame, ignorance and history.

## A Holocaust story centered on German suffering

Another point of controversy is the film’s focus on postwar German guilt. Michael, played as a young man by David Kross and later by Ralph Fiennes, belongs to the generation that inherited the knowledge of its parents’ crimes. His relationship with Hanna literalizes that inheritance: he is intimate with the past before he understands what it contains.

That idea reflects a significant strain in postwar German literature. Schlink’s novel is often read as an examination of the generation that came of age after the Third Reich and struggled with love, loyalty, disgust and judgment toward compromised elders.

But translating that theme into a Holocaust drama raises questions about whose trauma is foregrounded. Michael is not responsible for Hanna’s crimes, yet much of the film is devoted to his inability to form relationships after her disappearance and trial. Jewish suffering becomes the historical catastrophe behind his personal crisis.

The film does eventually bring Michael face to face with a Jewish survivor, played by Lena Olin, and the encounter sharply challenges any sentimental interpretation of Hanna. The survivor refuses to offer easy absolution or participate in a redemptive narrative. A tea tin Hanna once took from her is not transformed into a comforting symbol of reconciliation.

For supporters, that sequence restores the victims’ moral authority. For detractors, it arrives too late to rebalance a story already dominated by Hanna and Michael.

## Winslet’s performance complicates the question

Winslet’s Oscar-winning work is central to both the film’s acclaim and the discomfort surrounding it. She plays Hanna without reducing her to either a demon or a misunderstood innocent. Her physical reserve, flashes of anger and terror of exposure create a character whose private shame is palpable but whose moral reasoning remains profoundly limited.

That complexity made the performance awards-friendly, but it also sharpened the criticism. A charismatic star can generate sympathy even when a screenplay avoids overt exoneration. The better Winslet makes audiences understand Hanna’s fear and isolation, the more urgent the ethical question becomes: What is that understanding for?

The answer depends in part on whether viewers distinguish sympathy from absolution. Sympathy can mean recognizing another person’s emotions; absolution means releasing that person from responsibility. *The Reader* clearly does not acquit Hanna in legal terms. Whether it softens her in emotional terms is the controversy that has followed the film.

## Oscar recognition as cultural endorsement

Awards do not settle moral arguments, but they can magnify them. The Academy’s embrace of *The Reader* was viewed by admirers as recognition of ambitious filmmaking and a long-overdue honor for Winslet. To skeptics, the five nominations reflected Hollywood’s recurring attraction to prestige dramas that approach the Holocaust through the conscience, suffering or redemption of non-Jewish protagonists.

The best-picture nomination was especially striking because the film had received mixed-to-positive reviews rather than universal acclaim. Its awards campaign became part of the story, reinforcing perceptions that the movie had been positioned as a solemn, important work even as critics challenged its historical and ethical perspective.

Still, dismissing *The Reader* solely as “Oscar bait” can obscure why the debate persists. The film poses a genuine question with no comfortable answer: Can art enter the inner life of a perpetrator without displacing the people harmed by that perpetrator?

The answer may depend less on whether Hanna is portrayed sympathetically than on whether the film gives sufficient moral and imaginative space to her victims.

## A controversy that outlasted awards season

More than the nominations or Winslet’s victory, *The Reader* endures as a case study in the ethics of representation. It demonstrates that humanizing a perpetrator is not automatically the same as excusing one—but also that filmmakers cannot control how narrative intimacy distributes compassion.

Hanna’s illiteracy may explain her behavior in the courtroom and her lifelong secrecy. It does not explain, much less excuse, her service as a concentration-camp guard. The film’s most provocative choice is to make that distinction emotionally difficult rather than intellectually simple.

For some viewers, that difficulty is the point: moral responsibility matters precisely because guilty people can possess recognizable fears and vulnerabilities. For others, the film’s compassion is misallocated, turning the Holocaust into the backdrop for a perpetrator’s shame and a younger German man’s anguish.

That divide explains why *The Reader* remains more than an Oscar-winning literary adaptation. Its five nominations placed the film at the center of Hollywood’s biggest celebration, but they also ensured that its central ethical question would receive a much wider hearing: not whether a former Nazi guard may be portrayed as human, but what is lost when her humanity becomes the story’s most intimate concern.
